_note: Šablony příběhů. {placeholder} se doplní z vojáka/dne, [a|b|c] = náhodná volba. daily: váha w a podmínky line/archetype/weather. comrade/enemy: {a} a {b} jsou jména dvou skutečných hráčů (stejný text jde do záznamu obou, proto bez zájmen). arcs: vícedenní příběhové linky, kroky jdou po sobě s odstupem 1–3 dny, vars se vylosují jednou na začátku linky. weather: počasí dne (stejné pro celou frontu). Zájmena {he}/{his}/{him}/{He}/{His} podle vojáka.
items: a photograph gone soft at the edges
a book with the last pages torn out
a lock of hair in a matchbox
a pack of cards missing the queen of hearts
a child's drawing of a horse
a pocket Bible with a hole in it
a key to a house that is no longer there
enlist: {name} came up the line in the rain with {item} and nothing else. The sergeant wrote {him} down as {rank} and pointed at the mud.
Nobody saw {name} arrive. One morning there was simply one more helmet in {sector}, and a quiet {archetype} under it.
{name} signed the papers with a steady hand. The trench at {sector} took {him} in like it takes everyone: without a word.
They issued {name} a rifle, a spade and a number. {He} kept {item} in {his} breast pocket, where the shrapnel would have to go through it first.
{name} arrived with the evening ration party, carrying {item} and a borrowed greatcoat two sizes too big.
The new {archetype} gave {his} name as {name}. The corporal looked at {his} boots, then at the mud, and laughed for the first time in a week.
{name} stepped off the supply cart at {sector} and stood very still, listening to the guns as if they were saying {his} name.
Nobody asked {name} why {he} came. Nobody in {sector} asks that. {He} was handed a spade before {he} was handed a rifle.
{name} took the place of a man nobody would talk about. The dugout still had his blanket. {He} kept it folded.
{name} reported to {sector} with {item} sewn into {his} tunic lining. The sergeant pretended not to notice.

daily.text: Rain all night. {name} bailed water out of {sector} with a helmet until {his} hands stopped feeling anything.
{name} wrote a letter home. {He} wrote about the weather. {He} did not write about the rats.
On sentry duty {name} watched the wire for six hours. Twice {he} thought the wire watched back.
A flare lit {place} like noon. {name} counted the seconds until darkness: eleven.
{name} carried duckboards up from the rear all night. {His} shoulders are a map of splinters.
In reserve, {name} slept nine hours in a barn. {He} dreamt of nothing, which was the best part.
{name} traded {item} for two cigarettes and immediately regretted it.
The cook's stew tasted of iron and smoke. {name} ate two helpings anyway.
{name} spent the night underground, listening. Somewhere beneath {place} someone else was digging too.
{name} carried three men out of {sector} on a stretcher. One of them thanked {him}. Two could not.
{name} ran a message through the communication trench under shellfire. The message said: 'Hold.'
{name} lay in the ruins of {place} from dawn to dusk. {He} did not fire once. That is also a kind of victory.
{name} buried two men at the edge of {place} and said the words twice, because the shells interrupted the first time.
{name} cleaned the gun for the fourth time today. The gun is the only thing in the trench that is kept dry.
{name} made soup from what the rats left. The men called it the best soup on the front, and they were not joking.
A shell landed close to {sector}. When the dust settled {name} was still there, holding {item}, laughing without sound.
{name} found a flower growing out of a sandbag. {He} did not tell anyone. {He} checks on it every morning.
A crow sat on the parapet above {name} all afternoon. The men say it chose {him}.
The rain did not stop once. {name} slept standing up, wedged against the wall of {sector}, and dreamt of dry socks.
{name} lost a boot to the mud at {sector}. It took two men and a rifle sling to get it back. The mud kept the sock.
Water rose to the second step of the dugout. {name} moved {item} to the highest shelf and sat beside it like a guard.
Fog so thick that {name} could not see the end of {his} own rifle. Somewhere out there, someone was whistling.
In the fog a figure walked along the parapet of {sector}. When {name} challenged it, there was nobody there.
The fog lifted at noon and {name} saw {place} clearly for the first time. {He} wished it had stayed.
Frost on the wire made it sing in the wind. {name} could not stop listening to it.
{name} woke with {his} hair frozen to the sandbags. The cook brought tea so hot it hurt. Nobody complained.
The mud froze hard overnight. For one morning {name} could walk on top of it, like a man walking on water.
A clear sky. {name} kept {his} head low all day: on clear days the snipers do not miss.
Sun on {sector}. {name} took off {his} boots for the first time in nine days and the whole bay applauded.
Clear night. {name} counted stars until a flare went up and drowned them all.
Lightning lit {place} and {name} saw the enemy wire, the enemy trench, and a man in it looking straight back.
Thunder all night. {name} kept flinching. The old hands said that is how you tell the new ones: they flinch at God.
The east wind brought the smell of the other trenches: smoke, lime and somebody's cooking. {name} was hungry and furious about it.
The wind tore a sheet of corrugated iron off the dugout roof at {sector}. {name} chased it halfway down the communication trench.
{name} spent the night filling sandbags. By dawn {he} could no longer close {his} hands. By noon the shells had emptied half of them again.
{name} had a letter from home. {He} read it four times and then once more out loud, for the men who never get any.
A rat stole {name}'s cheese ration while {he} watched. {He} let it. The rat looked hungrier.
{name} was on wiring party in no man's land. Every time a flare went up {he} froze like a scarecrow. It worked.
{name} lost at cards to the corporal and now owes him a week of tobacco and one favour, unspecified.
Rumour reached {sector} that the war would be over by spring. {name} has heard it before. So has everyone.
{name} carved {his} initials into the trench wall next to a hundred others. Some of them are only half finished.
{name} spent the afternoon delousing {his} shirt over a candle. The lice won on points.
{name} sang under {his} breath on sentry. Across the wire, very quietly, somebody sang the next line.
A shell hit the latrine at {sector}. Nobody was hurt. {name} says it was the best day of the war.
Officers came to inspect {sector}. {name} polished {his} buttons with mud, which is the only polish there is.
{name} found an old map of {place} from before the war. There was a school on it, and an orchard. {He} looked for them. {He} did not find them.
{name} turned a year older today. The bay sang for {him}, badly, and the cook found a candle.
{name} saw a hare run the whole length of no man's land and nobody on either side fired at it.
{name} stood to at dawn with the rest of {sector}, bayonet fixed, staring into the grey. Nothing came. Nothing came yesterday, either.
Listening post, three in the morning. {name} heard boots, then whispering, then nothing. Just a fox, the corporal said. {He} did not sleep afterwards.
A trench raid went out from {sector}. {name} waited at the gap in the wire, counting heads as they came back.
{name} hauled ammunition boxes up the communication trench all night. {His} back filed a formal complaint.
{name} repaired a collapsed traverse at {sector} with sandbags, boards and language not fit for letters home.
Behind the lines {name} had a bath in a beer vat with eleven other men. The water was brown before {he} got in.
In the reserve billet {name} played football against the sappers. The ball was a sandbag stuffed with straw. The sappers cheated.
{name} drew the counter-mine plans by candlelight. Below {place} the earth is now a maze, and {he} knows every turn.
{name} set a charge under the enemy listening post. Then {he} waited all night for an order that did not come.
{name} splinted a broken leg with a rifle and two puttees. The patient asked if {he} was a real doctor. {He} said yes. {He} was lying.
The aid post ran out of morphine at four. {name} held a boy's hand until six. Then {he} went back for the next one.
{name} ran six messages in one night. The last one was a request for more runners.
{name} took the long way round {place} because the short way had a sniper on it. The long way had two.
{name} spent the day watching one loophole in the enemy line. At dusk a periscope rose in it. {He} let it go. Tomorrow.
{name} moved {his} hide three times today. Snipers who stay in one place do not stay anywhere for long.
The machine gun jammed at the worst moment. {name} cleared it with a bent nail and words the chaplain pretended not to hear.
{name} fired three short bursts at nothing to keep the enemy honest. The enemy fired three back to keep {him} honest too.
The telephone wire to {sector} was cut by shelling four times. {name} crawled out and spliced it four times.
{name} sent a pigeon back to headquarters. The pigeon came back two hours later. {name} took it personally.
{name} flashed a lamp signal to the battery behind the ridge. The answer came back: a single word, misspelled.
The cook's fire went out in the rain. {name} relit it under {his} own greatcoat and served stew that tasted of wool.
{name} carried hot tea up to the front line in petrol cans. Everyone could taste the petrol. Everyone drank it.
{name} held a service in a shell hole. Eleven men came. Two of them had never prayed before. Both of them asked for another.
{name} wrote letters for men who could not write, and some for men who could but did not know the words.
{name} studied the trench map until the candle died, then walked {sector} in the dark to learn it by heart.
{name} had orders to attack at dawn. {He} wrote back asking for artillery first. The orders were cancelled. Nobody knows which of {his} words did it.
{name} censored the men's letters tonight. {He} crossed out the place names and left in all the love.

promotion: For keeping {his} head when others lost theirs at {place}, {name} was promoted to {rank}.
The old {oldRank} did not come back from the wire. {name} wears {his} stripes now: {rank}.
{name} brought back a wounded man and a lost machine gun from {place} in one trip. {He} is {rank} now.
Nobody else in {sector} wanted the stripes. {name} said yes. {rank}.
The colonel asked who held the line at {place} last night. Every finger pointed at {name}. {rank}.
{name} was made {rank}. {He} celebrated by sleeping four hours in a row.
wounded: Shrapnel at {place}. {name} walked to the aid post on {his} own feet and asked for a cigarette before the stitches.
{name} was caught by gas at {sector}. {He} coughs in {his} sleep but swears {he} will be back on the line within the week.
A rifle grenade burst above {sector}. {name} took a splinter in the arm and refused to leave until the next man was bandaged.
{name} was buried by a shell at {place}. They dug {him} out after twenty minutes, deaf in one ear and still holding {item}.
Trench foot. {name} can no longer feel {his} toes and the medical officer has ordered {him} to the rear, swearing at the mud.
{name} was hit by a sniper at {place}. The bullet went through {his} shoulder and, somehow, missed everything that mattered.
A fever swept through {sector}. {name} was carried out shaking and talking to people who were not there.
Barbed wire at {place} opened {name}'s leg from knee to ankle. {He} limped back in carrying the wire-cutters, as ordered.
recovered: {name} is back from the field hospital, thinner and quieter, with {item} still in {his} pocket.
{name} came back to {sector} with a new scar and an old joke. The bay was glad of both.
The field hospital let {name} go. {He} came back up the line on foot because the lorry would not wait.
{name} returned from hospital carrying letters, chocolate and rumours, and handed out all three.
Back with {his} platoon, {name} found that someone had kept {his} place on the fire step. Nobody admitted who.
fallen: {name} fell at {place}. They found {item} in {his} pocket and sent it home with a letter that said {he} was brave. It was true.
The wire at {place} took {name}. {His} friends in {sector} carved {his} name into a duckboard so the mud would remember {him}.
{name} went over the top at {place} and did not come back. The roll was called twice. Nobody answered for {him}.
A shell found {name} in the dugout at {sector}. The men put {his} helmet on a cross by the road. It is still there.
{name} died at the aid post at dawn, holding {item}. The chaplain says {he} was smiling. The chaplain says that about everyone, but this time it was true.
{name} was lost in the mine explosion under {place}. There was nothing to bury. They buried {his} name instead.
heir: {name} came to the front because {his} {relation} {prevName} never came home. {He} carries {item}.
The papers say {name}. The sergeant says {he} has {his} {relation}'s eyes. {prevName}'s eyes. Nobody in {sector} argues.
A letter came with {name}: "I am {prevName}'s {relation}. I have come to finish what {he} started." Nobody had the heart to tell {him} it never finishes.
{name} took the same post at {sector} where {prevName} stood. {He} found {his} {relation}'s initials carved in the wall and put {his} own beneath them.
The House of {family} sent another. {name}, {relation} of {prevName}, arrived with the same eyes and the same stubborn silence.
missing: {name} went out with a patrol to {place} and did not come back with it. {He} is listed as missing. The men leave {his} rations untouched.
After the raid on {place}, {name} was not at the roll call. Somebody saw {him} in a shell hole. Somebody else says that was someone else.
{name} took a message across {place} at dusk. The message arrived. {name} did not.
returned: {name} crawled back into {sector} at dawn after two nights in a shell hole at {place}, covered in mud and carrying {item}. {He} asked if {he} had missed breakfast.
The sentry nearly shot {name} coming in through the wire. {He} had been lost in the fog at {place}, living on rainwater and stubbornness.
{name} turned up at a neighbouring battalion, having walked the wrong way for a day and a half. {He} came home to {sector} with three new friends and no explanation.
comrade: {a} and {b} shared the last tin of bully beef in the bay, counting the bites out loud to keep it fair.
{a} kept watch so that {b} could sleep. Then {bs} kept watch so that {as} could. Neither slept.
{a} taught {b} to play the harmonica. The bay has asked them both, formally, to stop.
{a} pulled {b} out of a flooded shell hole at {place}. Neither of them has mentioned it since. Both of them remember.
{a} and {b} argued all night about whose home town has the better beer. The argument has been adjourned until after the war.
{a} cut {b}'s hair with a bayonet and a cracked mirror. It is not good. It is, however, short.
{a} wrote a letter for {b}'s mother, because {bs} could not find the words. {bs} signed it.
{a} and {b} carved a chessboard into an ammunition box. The pieces are bullets, buttons and one very patient beetle.
{a} and {b} made a pact on sentry tonight: whoever gets home first visits the other's family. They shook on it with frozen hands.
{a} saw {b} freeze on the fire step at {place}. {as} said nothing, just stood closer. It was enough.
enemy: At {place}, {a} of the {af} and {b} of the {bf} traded insults across the wire for an hour. By the end they were trading recipes.
{a} ({af}) and {b} ({bf}) met in the same shell hole at {place} during a raid. They stared at each other. Then each crawled home, and neither has told anyone.
{b} of the {bf} threw a tin of tobacco into the {af} trench with a note: "for the one who sings". {a} kept the tin.
{a} had {b} of the {bf} in {his} sights at {place} for a long second. {b} was lighting a pipe. {a} let the match burn all the way down.
A football came over the parapet from the {bf} side with {b}'s name scratched on it. {a} kicked it back. It did not come again.
On a quiet night {a} ({af}) and {b} ({bf}) called out their names across no man's land, just to hear another voice. Now each knows exactly who is out there.

steps: A rat has started sitting on the ammunition box next to {name}'s bunk. {He} has named it {pet}.
{pet} the rat now waits for {name} at stand-to every morning. {He} shares crumbs with it. The corporal calls this desertion of rations.
{pet} ran squealing out of the dugout at three in the morning. {name} followed, cursing, seconds before a shell came through the roof. {He} owes {pet} {his} life.
{name} has not seen {pet} for two days. {He} tells everyone rats come and go. {He} still leaves crumbs on the box.
{name} got a letter from {love}. Two pages, one of them only about the weather back home. {He} read that page most.
{name} wrote back to {love} and tore it up three times. The fourth version says almost nothing, which is how {he} knows it is the right one.
No post for {name} this week. {He} checks the sack anyway, every day, and pretends {he} was only looking for tobacco.
A parcel from {love}: socks, a cake gone hard as a brick, and a pressed flower. {name} ate the cake and kept the flower in {item}'s place.
A one-eyed crow landed on the parapet above {name}. The men named it {crow} and said it had chosen {him}.
{crow} the crow follows {name} along the trench now. When {crow} flies off, men duck. They are usually right to.
Somebody in {sector} wanted to shoot {crow} for the pot. {name} stood in front of the rifle. The matter has been dropped.
A muddy dog crawled into {sector} through the wire. {name} gave it half {his} bread. It has not left {his} side since. The men call it {dog}.
{dog} has learned to carry messages in a tin on its collar. {name} is very proud. {dog} is mainly proud of the biscuits.
{dog} barked at nothing in the dark at four in the morning, and kept barking. A raiding party was twenty yards from the wire. {sector} was ready for them.
{name} hummed an old song from home on sentry. From the other side of the wire, very faintly, someone hummed it back.
{name} sang the first verse tonight, out loud. The other side sang the second. Nobody fired for an hour.
An officer heard about the singing and forbade it. Tonight {name} only whistled the first bar. Across the wire, someone whistled the last.

stranger: a woman in a white dress
two small boys on a bench
an old man with a dog

steps: {name} found a photograph in the mud of no man's land: {stranger}, and a name on the back that is not from {his} side of the wire.
{name} keeps the photograph in {his} pocket next to {item}. {He} says {he} will give it back after the war. Nobody asks to whom.
{name} left the photograph on a stake in the wire at {place}, wrapped in oilcloth. In the morning it was gone. In its place: a single cigarette.

stake: a pocket watch that does not work

steps: {name} won {stake} at cards from a lance corporal in {sector}. The lance corporal wants a rematch.
Rematch. {name} lost everything {he} won, plus {item}. The whole dugout watched.
Third game, by candlelight, with the shelling for a clock. {name} won back {item} and nothing else. {He} says that was all {he} was playing for.
{name} pressed {his} ear to the tunnel wall under {place} and heard it: tapping. Someone is digging toward {him}.
The tapping under {place} is closer. {name} and two others work in silence, in socks, by the light of one candle.
{name} broke through into the enemy gallery at dawn. It was empty. A lamp was still warm. {He} blew it out and placed the charge.
The mine under {place} went up at noon. The whole front felt it. {name} sat at the tunnel mouth afterwards and did not speak until dark.
There is a sniper across the way the men call {foe}. Three helmets went up on sticks today. {foe} hit all three. {name} watched where the shots came from.
{name} lay in the ruins of {place} all day. {foe} did not fire once. Neither did {name}. Both of them know.
At dusk a glint from the ridge. {name} fired once. The front has been quiet ever since, and nobody talks about {foe} any more.
{name} carried in {boy}, who lied about his age to enlist. {boy} kept asking whether his mother would be told.
{boy} has a fever. {name} sits with him after every shift and reads to him from a book with the last pages missing.
{boy} was put on the hospital train today, alive. He gave {name} a button from his tunic. {name} wears it on {his} own.
{name} learned that {prize} is stored in the cellar at battalion headquarters. {He} has been making careful drawings.
{name} volunteered for a supply run to headquarters. {He} came back with exactly what was ordered and a suspiciously large greatcoat.
The whole of {sector} ate well tonight. {prize} has been reported missing. {name} has been reported as a very good cook.
The line to the battery keeps going dead at the same spot near {place}. {name} suspects it is not the shelling.
{name} crawled out along the wire at night and found the break: neat, cut, recent. Someone is listening in.
{name} laid a second line, deep, by a different route, and left the old one live with false orders on it. Tomorrow the enemy shells an empty farm.
{name} started keeping a diary in the back of a field service book. First entry: "Still here."
{name}'s diary, day nine: "Still here. Rain. A rat called the Major. Nothing else worth writing, which is the point."
{name} read {his} diary from the start tonight and laughed at how frightened {he} was back then. Then {he} stopped laughing and wrote: "Still here."

weather.label: Rain
diary: It rained from dusk to dawn. The communication trenches are knee-deep again and the duckboards float.
Rain all day, steady and patient. The mud has swallowed two more boots and a mule.

weather.label: Fog
diary: Fog sat in the valley until noon. Sentries on both sides fired at shapes that were not there.
A grey wall of fog from dawn to dusk. Patrols went out blind and came back counting each other twice.

weather.label: Frost
diary: A hard frost. The mud froze into ridges sharp enough to cut boots, and the wire sang in the wind.
Ice on the water in the shell holes. The men stamped their feet all night to keep the blood moving.

weather.label: Clear
diary: A clear, cold day. Good for snipers and observers, bad for everyone else.
Blue sky over the front for the first time in a week. Both sides used it to shell each other with great accuracy.

weather.label: Storm
diary: Thunder all night, and nobody could tell which of it was the sky.
A storm broke over the ridge at midnight. Lightning showed the whole front for a heartbeat at a time: wire, craters, men.

weather.label: Wind
diary: A cold wind from the east carried the smell of the other trenches: smoke, lime and cooking.
Gale all day. Sandbags slid, roofs lifted, and the gas sentries watched the wind direction like hawks.
